By my manual count (no software run, so figures are approximate), Asian male applicants were denied in roughly 22 of about 180-190 applications, or about 11-12%. That is slightly above the overall rate of roughly 8-9% and above White applicants (about 6-7%), but below Hispanic or Latino applicants (about 13-15%). Most Asian male denials coincide with high debt-to-income ratios (>60% or 50%-60%) or very low or zero reported income. Asian male applicants with similar DTI, income and LTV profiles were mostly approved, so the data show no clear sign that being Asian and male drove denials. The gap is small, and a summary table without controls cannot rule out a modest effect.

I estimated these figures by reading the table, not by exact counts. Asian applicants, including Asian males, are denied at roughly 8-10% of applications. This is about the same as White applicants (roughly 7-9%) and Hispanic applicants (roughly 9-11%), and Asian approval rates are not lower than other groups'. Most denials in every group, including Asian males, occur with very high debt-to-income ratios (50%-60% or >60%) or very high loan-to-value ratios (95% or more). Asian males with moderate ratios were mostly approved, though a few were denied, as were some White and Hispanic applicants with similar profiles. The data shows no clear group-level pattern of disadvantage for Asian males. It does not control for credit score or other factors, so the confidence is moderate.
